duces to ranking units by their probability of being evidence. The
ranker therefore learns item relevance from gold labels, and with
𝐿=0it uses cheap features, as recommender cascades do.Agent-
MemRecuses a LightGBM model [20] trained with the LambdaRank
objective [4, 41]. Each (question, pooled turn) pair has ten features.
Five are cheap relevance signals: the bge-m3 cosine, the logarithms
of the global dense and BM25 ranks, the position in the fused pool
and the bge-reranker-v2-m3 cross-encoder score. Five describe the
turn: whether its role is user, its relative position in its session,
the logarithms of its age in days and of its length, and the spaCy
keys it shares with the question. The labels are the gold annota-
tions of the 152 development questions, with pools from both their
LongMemEval-S and LongMemEval-M

Long-term memory often contains personal, proprietary, or task-sensitive informa-
tion. Multi-user, multi-agent, and edge–cloud settings require access control, prove-
nance tracking, permission-aware retrieval, conflict management, secure deletion, and
privacy-preserving personalized memory management (Chen et al. 2026c). Paramet-
ric memory is especially challenging because a single remembered fact may not be
directly inspectable or removable. Practical memory systems should therefore expose
deletion logs, memory scopes, user consent controls, and policy-aware retrieval filters.
24
These governance mechanisms should be treated as core technical components rather
than deployment afterthoughts.

Current benchmarks cover long-context retrieval, conversational memory, multimodal
understanding, and simulation environments, but evaluation remains fragmented.
Future benchmarks should measure memory write quality, update correctness, absten-
tion, hallucinated memory use, privacy leakage, temporal consistency, and downstream
task success. They should also distinguish between genuine memory use and success
through long-context pattern matching. One practical approach is to evaluate agents
under controlled memory ablations, where memory contents are removed, corrupted,
delayed, or replaced to test whether the model truly depends on the intended memory
mechanism.
